items.author: secretsofuniverse
items.text:
🌗 Astronomers have found a dead star with two completely different faces.

The object is a white dwarf called ZTF J203349.8+322901.1, about 1,300 light-years away in Cygnus.

White dwarfs are the dense leftover cores of stars like the Sun. They pack roughly a star’s worth of mass into a body about the size of Earth.

But this one is unlike any white dwarf seen before.

As it spins once every 15 minutes, its spectrum changes dramatically.

When one side faces Earth, astronomers see hydrogen. When the other side rotates into view, they see helium.

That is why the team nicknamed it Janus, after the two-faced Roman god of transition.

The star is probably caught during a rare phase in white dwarf evolution, when its outer atmosphere is changing from hydrogen-dominated to helium-dominated as it cools.

Normally, this transition should happen across the whole star.

But Janus seems split in half.

The leading idea is that a weak magnetic field may be controlling how material mixes across its surface, allowing helium to rise on one side while hydrogen remains on the other.

It is a strange glimpse of a dying star mid-transformation.

A cosmic corpse with two faces, turning every 15 minutes.

📄 RESEARCH PAPER
📌 Caiazzo et al., “A rotating white dwarf shows different compositions on its opposite faces”, Nature (2023)

items.author: ryanhallyall
items.text:
It's official. June, July and August were the hottest summer in American history.

And it only set a record in four states.

1936 set records in eight and still lost, because New England and Florida ran cool that year. This summer not one state ran cool.

1936 still has the hottest afternoons on record. This summer beat it at night. Nights across the country were the warmest in 132 years.

If your afternoons felt normal but your house never cooled off after dark, that was it.

SEPT 11, 2001 | The satellite image of the U.S. Northeast Coast is one for the history books on Sept. 11, 2001. 

While New York City was in a state of emergency & the rest of the world was trying to come to grips with what happened, a massive hurricane was just offshore: Erin. 

On the morning of Sept. 11, 2001, Erin was large, with a giant eye. Winds were 90 mph & the hurricane was beginning to turn toward the northeast, away from the U.S.

The reason for the turn? A cold front had moved through the Northeast the day before. North winds behind the front brought drier, more comfortable conditions. It also cleared out the sky, giving New York those deep blue skies seen in all videos from that day. 

North winds behind the front pushed the smoke from the Twin Towers south. The smoke was so pronounced that when zooming in to the NASA satellite image of Erin below, you can actually see it moving south into New York Harbor & New Jersey.   

A weather image that will forever be part of American history. 

#sept11 #911 #newyork #hurricane #hurricaneerin

items.text:
Well, it’s official! As of this posting (10 am on 9/11) the 2026 Atlantic hurricane season has gone longer without producing its first hurricane than any other season in the modern satellite era, which began in 1966.

Even more remarkable, there isn’t a tropical wave or disturbance of concern on the horizon. That means a hurricane is unlikely to form for at least another week, and perhaps considerably longer. There’s even a decent chance we make it through the entire month of September without one.

With so much weather doom, gloom and hype running rampant on social media, it’s refreshing to report a record for inactivity instead of intensity.

Enjoy the calm! 🌀❌

items.text:
WHERE WERE YOU 25 YEARS AGO TODAY?
🇺🇸🇺🇸🇺🇸🇺🇸🇺🇸

On September 11, 2001, I was on a flight from Myrtle Beach to Charlotte when the Twin Towers were struck. I had no idea what had happened until I stepped off the plane and saw crowds gathered around TVs in silence. As we all watched in shock, word came that another plane had hit the Pentagon. A chill went through me, and the sound of a collective gasp filled the concourse.

No one felt safe. Many were terrified that Charlotte’s airport could be next, and honestly, it didn’t feel impossible. My final destination didn’t matter anymore…the skies were shut down. Later that morning, I walked out of one of the nation’s busiest airports into an eerie quiet, no jet engines, no takeoffs, no landings. Just silence.

Like millions of others, I spent the rest of the day glued to the television, watching in disbelief. I had never experienced anything like it, and I hope we never do again.

Twenty-five years later, I still pray for every life lost that day and for the families who continue to grieve. I also think of the thousands who have given their lives since then defending our freedom, and I pray for them and their families too.

9/11 was a moment when America came together, united in sorrow and patriotism. I wish we still held that same closeness today.

🇺🇸#NeverForget 🇺🇸

items.text:
PNW SATURDAY STORMS⛈️a compact upper-level low will move inland across southwestern Washington and northwestern Oregon Saturday, bringing widespread showers and unusually cold air aloft. As the colder air moves over the relatively milder surface, temperatures will decrease rapidly with height, creating steeper lapse rates and increasing atmospheric instability. This setup can support scattered thunderstorms capable of lightning, brief heavy rain, gusty winds and small hail.

The circulation around the low will also increase localized low-level wind shear and spin in the atmosphere. Convergence boundaries beneath the low could concentrate that rotation, allowing stronger shower updrafts to stretch it vertically and produce cold-air funnel clouds. Most cold-air funnels remain weak and never reach the ground, but an isolated brief touchdown cannot be ruled out, especially near the coast or over the open waters of the Pacific.

If you have outdoor plans, such as hiking, camping or boating, be prepared for storms and move indoors and off water quickly if storms approach⛈️

items.author: secretsofuniverse
items.text:
🧬 Scientists have found life-related sugars inside samples from asteroid Bennu.

The samples were collected by NASA’s OSIRIS-REx mission, which touched asteroid Bennu in 2020 and returned its material safely to Earth in 2023.

Now, researchers have found several bio-essential sugars inside that pristine asteroid dust.

The most important one is ribose, the sugar used to build RNA.

That matters because RNA is central to one major origin-of-life idea called the RNA world, where early life may have relied on RNA before DNA became the main genetic storage molecule.

The Bennu sample also contained glucose, one of the most common energy sources used by life on Earth.

This does not mean Bennu was alive.

It means the chemistry needed for life was already happening inside ancient asteroid material formed more than 4.5 billion years ago.

The discovery builds on earlier Bennu findings of amino acids, phosphate, ammonia and all five nucleobases used by DNA and RNA.

Together, these results are making one idea harder to ignore.

Asteroids may have helped deliver the raw molecular toolkit from which life on Earth began.

📄 RESEARCH PAPER
📌 Furukawa et al., “Bio-essential sugars in samples from asteroid Bennu”, Nature Geoscience (2025)

Did it feel hotter than normal this summer? ☀️ Utah, Colorado and New Mexico experienced their hottest summers in 132 years of recorded weather. Arizona tied for its record warmest summer, according to NOAA data from June, July and August.

These states experienced temperatures more than 5 degrees higher than the historical average.

The Lower 48 states averaged 76.9 degrees in July, breaking records dating to 1895 and surpassing the extreme heat of July 1936 during the Dust Bowl. Multiple heat domes sent temperatures soaring across the country, while drought and dry soil allowed the ground to heat more efficiently.

items.text:
🌌 A dark matter detector nearly a mile underground has recorded a signal scientists cannot yet explain.

The signal came from LUX-ZEPLIN, or LZ, one of the world’s most sensitive dark matter experiments.

It sits deep beneath South Dakota inside the Sanford Underground Research Facility, shielded from cosmic rays by nearly a mile of rock.

At its heart are tonnes of ultra-pure liquid xenon, waiting for the faint flash that could be caused by a dark matter particle.

In a new analysis, researchers studied 220 live days of data collected between March 2023 and April 2024.

They found one event that looked like a nuclear recoil of about 248 keV.

That means something appears to have struck a xenon nucleus and made it recoil.

The strange part is that the event appeared in a region where ordinary background signals should be very rare.

If it was caused by dark matter, the particle may be a WIMP at least 200 times heavier than a proton.

But one event is not a discovery.

The signal currently stands at 2.6 sigma, meaning it could still be a rare background event.

For now, LZ has not found dark matter.

But it may have found its most interesting hint yet.

📄 RESEARCH PAPER
📌 Akerib et al., “Search for dark matter particle interactions in an extended nuclear recoil energy window with the LUX-ZEPLIN (LZ) experiment”, arXiv preprint, submitted to Physical Review Letters (2026)

🍄 Psilocybin may help prevent one of chemotherapy’s most painful side effects — but so far, only in preclinical models.

Chemotherapy-induced peripheral neuropathy can cause numbness, tingling, pain, cold sensitivity, and loss of sensation in the hands and feet.

It can last long after treatment and sometimes forces doctors to reduce or stop life-saving chemotherapy.

In a new study, researchers gave mice psilocybin before chemotherapy. As few as two doses protected them from nerve damage across several chemotherapy models, including cisplatin, paclitaxel, and docetaxel.

The drug appeared to protect nerve endings by preserving mitochondrial movement inside nerve fibers, helping cells maintain their energy supply.

Importantly, psilocybin did not weaken chemotherapy’s anti-tumor effect in the models tested.

This is promising, but not proven in humans. Clinical trials are now needed.

📃 RESEARCH PAPER
📌 Heles et al., “Psilocybin prevents chemotherapy-induced peripheral neuropathy through mitochondrial trafficking preservation”, Science (2026)

The wreckage beneath Oppenheimer’s foot once held the world’s first atomic bomb.

#TBT #ThrowBackThursday

On September 9, 1945, J. Robert Oppenheimer and General Leslie Groves returned to ground zero at the Trinity site in New Mexico. Oppenheimer rests one foot on the remains of the steel tower that supported the device.

Nearly two months earlier, on July 16, the first nuclear explosion had destroyed that tower. The Manhattan Project had demonstrated that its plutonium bomb worked.

By the time this photograph was taken, atomic bombs had been dropped on Hiroshima and Nagasaki, and Japan had surrendered.

Oppenheimer had directed the Los Alamos laboratory; Groves had commanded the project. Here, both stand beside the physical remains of the test that preceded those bombings.

Even better, the tropics are completely quiet right now, with nothing expected to develop over the next 7–10 days. If that continues, there's at least a chance we could make it all the way to the end of September without a hurricane.

items.author: JeffBerardelli
items.text:
‼️ Dust Bowl, left in the Dust!
Climate contrarians love to cherry pick summer of 1936 in the US. But zoom out…
Summer 1936 was about 1.36°C or 2.45°F cooler 🥶 globally, than 2026.
Some context: US Summer 1936 was extreme in the plains Dust Bowl and adjacent areas. In fact, nearly half of U.S. states still have an all-time record high temp that was set during the Dust Bowl era.
The warming was localized to the US, but the warm bubble helped establish a high amplitude quasi stationary wave pattern in the Summer of 1936 (bottom map) across the northern hemisphere. If you look closely you can see the pattern of warm, cool, warm, cool, warm from the US-Atlantic - Europe. Some of the Dust Bowl was caused by poor human farming practices, and mowing down of native prairie grass, which shows you how humans can indeed impact the large scale climate. Impressive. But if you look closely enough at 1936 you can see a cold pool over the eastern Pacific, which helped establish the overall atmospheric wave pattern. Hand in hand, nature and humans worked to make the 1930s summers in the Plains intolerable. 
But zoom out and you’ll see human-caused global warming dwarfs the Dust Bowl. Modern climate change is global. Dust Bowl heat was mainly regional. 
Data: ERA & Berkeley Earth.

On September 10, 2008, the Large Hadron Collider fired up for the very first time, sending a beam of protons racing all the way around its 27-kilometre ring buried beneath the border of France and Switzerland.

It's the biggest and most complex machine humans have ever built, and that morning, after decades of planning and construction, engineers watched a single dot of light confirm the beam had made the full loop. The control room broke into applause.

The doomsday fears were never taken seriously by physicists. The collisions the LHC produces happen naturally when cosmic rays hit our atmosphere, and Earth has survived those for billions of years.

Just nine days later, an electrical fault caused serious damage and shut the collider down for over a year. But it recovered. And in 2012, the LHC delivered what it was built for: the discovery of the Higgs boson, the particle that gives mass to matter.

Today it's still running, still smashing particles together, still hunting for whatever lies beyond the physics we currently understand.

🔥 Betelgeuse’s fiery, bubbling face has been seen in stunning detail.

Using ALMA, astronomers have imaged the inner atmosphere of Betelgeuse, the famous red supergiant in Orion that will one day explode as a supernova.

Betelgeuse is so huge that if it replaced the Sun, its outer layers would reach far beyond the orbit of Mars.

That enormous size lets telescopes resolve features across its atmosphere, something we cannot do for most stars.

The new ALMA observations show that Betelgeuse is not a smooth glowing sphere.

Its atmosphere is distorted, corrugated and marked by giant hot patches.

One of these regions is about 800 K hotter than the surrounding gas.

Even stranger, the brightest hot spot appears in almost the same location as it did in ALMA data from 2015.

That means some structures in Betelgeuse’s atmosphere may survive for at least seven years, much longer than current models of giant convection predict.

These hot patches are likely linked to huge rising cells of gas that drive shocks through the star’s outer layers.

That matters because this violent activity may help Betelgeuse shed material into space before its final explosion.

We are not just seeing a star.

We are watching a dying giant change before our eyes.

📄 RESEARCH PAPER
📌 Dent et al., “ALMA high resolution observations of Betelgeuse: Persistent structure spanning the inner atmosphere”, Astronomy & Astrophysics (2026)

items.author: EdPiotrowskiWPDE

PEAK OF HURRICANE SEASON

Wind shear and dry air have slammed the door on tropical development! No tropical systems are expected to develop for at least 7 days. Gotta love it!

Today (September 10th) is the historical peak of hurricane season. It's the one day in 174 years of reliable records that you are most likely to have a tropical storm or hurricane in the Atlantic Ocean. While it's statistically all downhill from here, history tells us we can't let our guard down. We've had many huge hits from hurricanes after this date, including:

Cat. 1 Florence in 2018
Cat. 1 Matthew in 2016
Cat. 2 Floyd in 1999
Cat. 4 Hugo in 1989
Cat. 4 Hazel in 1954

The latest we've ever been hit was October 31st, 1899. That hurricane was a Category 2 that made landfall in Myrtle Beach. Bet that wasn't a good night for trick-or-treating!

This year is a little different because of El Niño. I’m certainly not saying we can’t get hit, but El Niño does tend to make it much harder for storms to develop and strengthen in our part of the Atlantic.

STORMS THURSDAY⛈️ a cold front will slowly push south across Oklahoma and toward North Texas tomorrow, bringing several rounds of scattered storms!

Rain and storms will be ongoing across parts of Oklahoma during the morning before additional storms develop along the front from late morning through the afternoon. The greatest coverage is expected across central and southern Oklahoma, where a few storms could become strong to severe with damaging wind gusts and locally heavy rain. Tulsa and northeastern Oklahoma also have a high chance of storms but weaker wind shear will limit the overall severe threat.

Storms will reach the Red River and North Texas during the afternoon and evening. Coverage around DFW will be more scattered with the highest coverage closer to the Red River. Not everyone will receive rain but any stronger storm could produce gusty winds, frequent lightning and a brief heavy downpour.

The overall flash flood threat remains isolated because of recent dry conditions but localized ponding or minor flooding can’t be ruled out beneath the strongest storms. Activity will gradually decrease Thursday night from west to east⛈️

ISS FLYOVER AT 8:30 PM

Despite some high clouds around, it should be a great evening to see the International Space Station fly overhead. Look up at 8:30 pm! If you've never seen it, the ISS looks like a bright point of light (as bright as Venus) moving steadily across the sky. It will appear in the southwest sky and then disappear in the northeast sky. In reality, the ISS is moving at over 17,500 mph and is 250 miles above us!

That brilliant “light” you see from the ground is not a headlight or other light on the ISS. You’re seeing sunlight reflected off the enormous station, particularly its solar arrays and other reflective surfaces. The solar arrays alone cover roughly half an acre.

NORTHWEST MOUNTAIN SNOW THIS WEEKEND | WINTER ALERTS POSSIBLE🏔️❄️confidence continues to increase in a cold early-season storm will bring the first impactful mountain snowfall of the season to parts of the Northwest and Northern Rockies this weekend! 

The strongest signal remains across Montana, where snow levels could fall to around 6,000 feet Saturday night into Sunday. The highest potential exists near Glacier National Park, the Rocky Mountain Front, Bitterroots and Continental Divide. There is now a high chance of 4-6 inches of snow along the Rocky Mountain Front and a potential for a foot for the highest peaks.
 
Snow levels could fall to around 7,000-8,000 feet across the central Idaho mountains and 7,000-8,500 feet in northwestern Wyoming, bringing snow to the highest portions of the Sawtooths, Tetons, Absarokas and Wind Rivers.

Washington and Oregon will also turn sharply cooler and wetter Saturday. Most lower elevations will receive rain and snow will reach the highest Cascade peaks, above 6,500 feet with light. accumulations above 7,500 feet. Temperatures across parts of Washington and Oregon will run 15-20°F below normal this weekend.

Anyone hunting, hiking or visiting the high country should prepare for a rapid change to cold, wet and potentially wintry conditions. Winter weather headlines may eventually be needed if confidence and forecast snowfall totals continue increasing🏔️❄️

Perfect Game Day weather today - GO HAWKS - but the weather begins to change by Friday, continuing into the weekend! Another strong early-season storm system will drop south out of western Canada and sweep across the Northwest and Northern Rockies Friday through Monday!

The system will first impact Washington and Oregon Friday into Saturday with increasing rain, sharply cooler temperatures and gusty winds, along with the highest peaks seeing snow. As the colder upper-level low moves inland Saturday, showers and scattered thunderstorms could develop across parts of Oregon, eastern Washington and Idaho.

By Saturday night and Sunday, the colder air spreads into Idaho, Montana and Wyoming. Temperatures will fall well below normal in parts of the region, with snow levels dropping enough for accumulating snow across some of the highest mountains. The strongest snow signal currently exists across Montana and Wyoming, including parts of the northern Rockies and northwest Wyoming.

The storm gradually shifts east Sunday into Monday, with Washington and Oregon beginning to dry out while cooler and unsettled weather lingers farther east🌧️❄️

items.author: secretsofuniverse
items.text:
🚀 Europe just opened a new route to space.

German startup Isar Aerospace has successfully launched its Spectrum rocket from Andøya Spaceport in northern Norway.

The mission, called Onward and Upward, lifted off on September 5, 2026, at 10:12 p.m. CEST.

A little over seven minutes later, Spectrum reached orbit.

That makes Isar Aerospace the first European commercial space company to successfully deliver satellites into orbit using its own launch vehicle.

The achievement is especially important because the launch happened from continental Europe.

Europe has launched rockets before, mainly from French Guiana in South America. But launching to orbit from European soil has been a much harder milestone.

Spectrum is a two-stage rocket, about 28 meters tall, designed to carry up to 1,000 kilograms to low Earth orbit.

This was only its second flight.

Its first test launch in March 2025 lasted about 30 seconds before the rocket fell into the sea. But Isar treated that as part of the learning curve, fixed the problem, and returned with a successful orbital mission.

This time, Spectrum carried five CubeSats and one experiment.

For Europe’s private space industry, this was more than a launch.

It was proof that a new commercial path to orbit has begun.

📄 MISSION
📌 Isar Aerospace, “History for European spaceflight: Isar Aerospace reaches orbit and deploys payloads on second flight”, Onward and Upward Mission, 2026

A front will stall across Oklahoma overnight, and an outflow boundary is expected to develop Thursday. This should help trigger scattered showers and thunderstorms near the Red River during the late afternoon and evening.

The highest coverage will be along the Red River at around 60%.

items.author: NTXWC
items.text:
The afternoon high-res data is in. Here is an idea of what kind of rainfall we might be dealing with on Thursday. 

I've drawn a zone, mainly situated northwest of the metroplex, where some locations could see rainfall totals over an inch. I have about a 60% coverage of showers and storms Thursday pm close to the Red River, with coverage gradually decreasing towards the metroplex (10-20%)

Now, as you can see, many places in the red circle may see nothing at all. That's the nature of storms this time of year- without large systems swinging through, storms don't move all that much, and don't stay organized for very long, leaving to scattered instances of heavy rainfall. So while I can't say for sure who will see a storm, those in the red circle and along the Red River have the highest chance to see brief downpours capable of multi-inch rainfall totals, lightning, and gusty winds. 

As for the metroplex, it depends how much outflow is produced and how far southeast it pushes.

It's certainly the best chance for rain we've seen since early July, but it won't provide much relief for most.

items.author: secretsofuniverse
items.text:
A mysterious low-frequency hum has been detected by pulsar timing arrays, networks of rapidly spinning neutron stars used as cosmic clocks.

The leading explanation is that this hum comes from pairs of supermassive black holes slowly spiraling together across the Universe.

But a new study asks a deeper question.

Where did the ancestors of those enormous black holes come from?

One possibility is Dark Stars, a hypothetical first generation of stars powered not mainly by nuclear fusion, but by energy linked to dark matter.

In some models, these objects could grow huge, reaching up to a million times the mass of the Sun before collapsing into massive black holes.

Over billions of years, those early black hole seeds could grow, merge with others, and eventually form the supermassive black hole binaries that generate today’s gravitational-wave background.

The researchers found that if Dark Star remnants were common enough, their descendants could make a major, possibly dominant, contribution to the signal detected by pulsar timing arrays.

This does not prove Dark Stars existed.

But it gives scientists a new way to test the idea.

A faint cosmic hum today may carry the aftershock of stars that formed more than 13 billion years ago.

📄 RESEARCH PAPER
📌 Ghodla et al., “Reconstructing PTA measurements via early seeding of supermassive black holes”, Physical Review D (2026)

items.author: MeteorologistChristopherNunley
items.text:
3 MORE TROPICAL AREAS TO WATCH IN THE PACIFIC🌴🌀🌊behind Lowell, Marie and Karina, the Pacific remains very active with three separate areas now being monitored for possible tropical development.

The most immediate is EP96, located south-southwest of Baja California. Organization continues to improve, and a tropical depression is expected to form later today or tonight as it tracks west-northwest at 10-15 mph. Development odds have climbed to 90% through both 48 hours and 7 days.

Farther east, another area of low pressure is forecast to form several hundred miles south of Baja this weekend or early next week. Gradual development is possible as it also moves west-northwest, with a 40% chance of tropical development during the next 7 days.

A third area is particularly worth watching for Hawaii. A l ow pressure is forecast to form south-southeast of the islands, with gradual development possible late this week into the weekend as it moves slowly north-northwest. Development odds currently sit at 20% over the next 7 days.

There is NO imminent tropical threat to Hawaii or Southern California from any of these systems right now. However, Hawaii and Southern California will need to monitor the tropics closely over the next week. Even systems that remain well offshore can eventually send long-period swells toward the islands or the Southern California coast, producing larger surf, stronger rip currents and potentially additional coastal impacts depending on their eventual strength, size and track. Lots to watch across the Pacific as we move deeper into September🌴🌀🌊
